In my implementation I don't clean the stack when popping a value. I just decrease the t register value.

After "int 0,4" t is increased by 4 and we see the last 4 values of the stack. The first 3 are just pushed by the procedure call and the 4th one is the local variable. As there is no default initialization, this one gets the value which is at that position from previous usages.

This is the reason of the fatal error later on. I did a buggy program where there is an infinite loop with "sto". As this instruction decreases t, then the stack is shrinking at each loop. So, 12 is there onto the stack at position b+3, but t value is 2. So, there are several reasons which could raise the Fatal Error. Either because you access a variable with an address over t, or in my case when t becomes negative.

My interpetation of your way of implementation (without looking at your Python code):

• Originally int 0, 5 allocates 2 variable spaces.

• An earlier sto 0, 3 eliminates 1 variable space in error when it pops address 4 and tries to store 6 at address 3.

• The current sto 0, 3 first pops 12 at address 3, and eliminates that variable space on the stack as well.

• Then it tries to store 12 at address 3, but no space is available.

• Shouldn't an error occur at that point, instead of even later?

That's my question 😉

Well it depends how the stack is implemented. There is no stack access rule. I agree that potentially we could raise an error. 

While running the program, there are many access in the stack over the [[t]] register. In real assembler, it would work with a risk of core dump. In my case, it does not break as the stack is a fixed size.

I don't have an issue with this, but if you prefer we can define a new rule such as "Any access to the stack outside boundaries [[0]]..[[t]] should raise a fatal error".

I have no preference. It's just necessary to set it out clear in the statement. So, it's

EITHER
The whole stack of 1024 positions are initialised with a value of 0, and the "int" instruction reinitialises the positions allocated to variables as 0. Stack access is always allowed even outside allocated positions. An error arises only when trying to access positions of absolute address less than 0 or greater than 1023.

OR
The whole stack of 1024 positions are not initialised, and the "int" instruction (re)initialises the positions allocated to variables as 0. Stack access is only allowed at allocated positions. Stack access at all other positions will raise an error.

Which one sounds more correct to you? Or are there other variations still?

May also have to critically review what should be done when popping a temp value from the stack, and when deallocating positions on returning from a call. Are the popped/deallocated positions zeroed out or left alone?

In my implementation, the stack is zeroed out also when returning from a call including all values which could have been push onto the stack (after variables allocation).

The whole stack of 1024 positions are initialised with a value of 0, and all positions allocated during a procedure call are reinitialised as 0 when returning from a call. Stack access is always allowed even outside allocated positions. An error arises only when trying to access positions of absolute address less than 0 or greater than 1023.

Thank you for the clarification. Please check if my understanding of the stack implementation below is correct or not:

Agreed:

A1. stack size = 1024

A2. accessing stack index 1024 or above => "stack overflow" error

A3. initialisation of whole stack at the start - zeroed out

A4. initialisation during stack allocation for variables when a procedure is called - zeroed out

A5. treatment of allocated stack positions when a procedure is terminated - zeroed out?

Agreed non-error scenarios:

E1. accessing a stack position which has been initialised but no value has ever been pushed (e.g. int 0, 4; lod 0, 3 => result = 0)

E2. accessing a stack position which has not been initialised and no value has ever been pushed (e.g. int 0, 3; lod 0, 9 => result = 0)

E3. accessing a stack position outside its frame (e.g. int 0, 4 in Frame 0, then int 0, 4 and lod 1, 5 in Frame 1 => result = value at absolute address 5)

E4. accessing a stack position which was previously initialised and a value was pushed, but then the procedure call has terminated (opr 0, 0), so the stack position is no longer attached to any active frame => result = 0

Clarification needed:

C1. How is pop done with `opr` (e.g. maths, comparison, printing) or `jpc` - is the popped stack position zeroed out?

C2. What "fatal error" covers: does it arise only when the [[t]] register becomes -1? Any other situations?

C3. Is this a non-error? Accessing a stack position which was previously initialised and a value was pushed but then popped (e.g. int 0, 3; lit 0, 8; lod 0, 3; lod 0, 3 => result = 0)

C4. Anything else I've missed?

A1. stack size = 1024

Yes

A2. accessing stack index 1024 or above => "stack overflow" error

Yes

A3. initialisation of whole stack at the start - zeroed out

Yes

A4. initialisation during stack allocation for variables when a procedure is called - zeroed out

Yes

A5. treatment of allocated stack positions when a procedure is terminated - zeroed out?

Yes (which then implies A4)

E1. accessing a stack position which has been initialised but no value has ever been pushed (e.g. int 0, 4; lod 0, 3 => result = 0)

Yes. No error, default initialization is 0.

E2. accessing a stack position which has not been initialised and no value has ever been pushed (e.g. int 0, 3; lod 0, 9 => result = 0)

Yes as well. There is a risk of fatal error but no restriction. This is the responsibility of the compiler to produce valid accesses.

E3. accessing a stack position outside its frame (e.g. int 0, 4 in Frame 0, then int 0, 4 and lod 1, 5 in Frame 1 => result = value at absolute address 5)

For me same as E2. There is no proactive monitoring of stack accesses. And again, it could lead to a fatal error.

E4. accessing a stack position which was previously initialised and a value was pushed, but then the procedure call has terminated (opr 0, 0), so the stack position is no longer attached to any active frame => result = 0

Ok as well. Same as for previous points. 

C1. How is pop done with `opr` (e.g. maths, comparison, printing) or `jpc` - is the popped stack position zeroed out?

Not in my solution. Values remains at their position in the stack, only t register is updated to point to the top value of the stack. Those values will be zeroed out while returning from the procedure.

C2. What "fatal error" covers: does it arise only when the [[t]] register becomes -1? Any other situations?

Any unexpected error while executing the program.

C3. Is this a non-error? Accessing a stack position which was previously initialised and a value was pushed but then popped (e.g. int 0, 3; lit 0, 8; lod 0, 3; lod 0, 3 => result = 0)

Yes this is a non-error. It very similar to questions in E.x section. This is a valid usage of PL/0 instructions which leads to a strange program. This should not happen if PL/0 instructions are generated by a valid PL/0 compiler. Only invalid programs may have those patterns which either could imply a FATAL Error (because of an unexpected error or an invalid stack access) or a Maximum Runtime Reach error (as an invalid usage of PL/0 instructions might create an infinite loop).

C4. Anything else I've missed?

Not to what I can see. Your review has been very deep and complete.

The exact circumstances leading to a fatal error must be specified, otherwise it's impossible for the players to know how they should solve the puzzle / when they should output that error. Defining "fatal" as "unexpected" does not provide any additional information. 😅

(That's also why I don't understand why there's a risk of fatal error you mentioned for E2, E3 and maybe E4.)

You are right and to be honest, it was more "in case of" for E2, E3 or E4 that I said it could lead to a FATAL Error. In the listed cases, it is true it should not.

So, we can stick to the "Fatal error" definition in goal.
